at regne.explanation: "At regne" means to rain. It is used with "det" (it): "det regner" is "it is raining". Danish does not need a separate "is raining" form, so one word covers both "it rains" and "it is raining". The word for the rain itself is "regn".

sentence.en: It is raining all day today.

at rejse.explanation: "At rejse" means to travel or to go away on a trip. "Jeg rejser til Danmark" means "I am travelling to Denmark". The "have" form uses "er" instead of "har": "Jeg er rejst" (I have left / travelled), because the word is about going from one place to another. Another useful word is "en rejse" (a trip).

sentence.en: I am travelling to Copenhagen tomorrow.

at ringe.explanation: "At ringe" means to call someone on the phone. You say "ringe til nogen": "Jeg ringer til dig i morgen" (I will call you tomorrow). It can also mean to ring, like a bell or a doorbell. A common phrase is "Ring til mig" (Call me).

sentence.en: I will call you tomorrow.

at ringe op.explanation: "At ringe op" means to phone someone. You put the person between the two parts: "jeg ringer dig op" (I call you up). The short form "at ringe til" someone is just as common: "jeg ringer til dig". When the phone rings, you say "telefonen ringer".

sentence.en: I will call you tomorrow.

at ringe til.explanation: "At ringe til" means to call someone on the phone. You need "til" (to) before the person: "Jeg ringer til min mor". If you just say "at ringe", it can also mean a bell ringing. A phone call itself is "et opkald".

sentence.da: Jeg **ringer til** min mor i aften.
sentence.en: I'm calling my mom tonight.

en rabat.explanation: "En rabat" means a discount, an amount taken off the price. You can ask "Kan jeg få rabat?" (Can I get a discount?), though in Denmark people do not haggle much in normal shops. Students, older people and members often get "rabat". "Rabatten" is the word for the discount.

sentence.da: Får jeg **rabat**, hvis jeg køber to?
sentence.en: Do I get a discount if I buy two?

en radio.explanation: "Radio" is the same idea as in English: a radio set, or the radio as a way of listening to news and music. You say "i radioen" for on the radio. It sounds close to English, but the Danish "r" is softer.

sentence.en: I listen to the radio in the car.

en recept.explanation: "En recept" is a prescription from a doctor, which you take to the pharmacy to get medicine. For a cooking recipe, "en opskrift" is the usual word.

sentence.da: Jeg skal have en **recept** fra lægen.
sentence.en: I need a prescription from the doctor.

en regning.explanation: En regning is a bill, either at a restaurant or one that you get at home, for example for electricity. The polite question in a restaurant is "Må jeg bede om regningen?" (May I ask for the bill?). In Danish, "the bill" is "regningen". In school the same word can also mean sums or arithmetic, but the bill meaning is the one you need most.

sentence.en: May I have the bill?

en regnjakke.explanation: "En regnjakke" is a rain jacket, built from "regn" (rain) and "jakke" (jacket). Danish weather changes quickly, so most people own one. Danish often builds new words by putting two words together, so you can guess many words like this. The word "the" goes on the end: "regnjakken".

sentence.en: Take your rain jacket with you, it is raining.

en regnskov.explanation: "Regnskov" is two words joined together: "regn" (rain) and "skov" (forest). Danish builds a lot of words this way, and the last part decides en or et: since it is "en skov", it is also "en regnskov". The plural is "regnskove".

sentence.da: Det regner hele året i en **regnskov**.
sentence.en: It rains all year in a rainforest.

en reje.explanation: "En reje" is a shrimp or prawn. You often use it in the plural, "rejer", because you usually eat several. Danes eat them on bread with mayonnaise, called "rejemad". Pay attention to the j, which sounds like a y: "RAI-eh".

sentence.da: Jeg vil have **rejer** på mit brød.
sentence.en: I want shrimps on my bread.

en rejse.explanation: "Rejse" is a trip or journey, usually a longer one far from home, such as a holiday abroad. It is also the verb "at rejse" (to travel). A short outing is more often "en tur". Danes say "God rejse!" to wish someone a good trip.

sentence.en: We have a trip to Spain.

en reservation.explanation: "Reservation" is a reservation, such as a table at a restaurant, a seat on a train or a hotel room. Danes say "Jeg har en reservation" (I have a reservation) or "at bestille bord" (to book a table). The verb is "at reservere".

sentence.en: I have a reservation tonight.

en restaurant.explanation: En restaurant is a restaurant, a place where you sit down and have a meal. Danes say "på restaurant" with no "en" for "at a restaurant" when they talk about eating out, and "at spise på restaurant" is the common way to say it. And "the restaurant" is "restauranten".

sentence.en: We are eating at a restaurant tonight.

en returbillet.explanation: "Returbillet" is a return ticket, one that takes you there and back again. The opposite is "en enkeltbillet" (one-way ticket). At a counter you can say "En returbillet til Aarhus, tak." Note the double t in the plural "returbilletter".

sentence.en: A return ticket to Aarhus, please.

en rose.explanation: "En rose" is a rose, the flower. Giving "roser" is a classic romantic gesture. The same word is also used for the colour pink in "rosa", which is a related word. A rose bush is "en rosenbusk".

sentence.en: He gave her a rose.

en ryg.explanation: "En ryg" is the back of your body. The y is a rounded sound, a bit like the French u. It is used for pain: "Jeg har ondt i ryggen" (My back hurts). "At ligge på ryggen" means to lie on your back.

sentence.en: My back hurts.

en rygsæk.explanation: "Rygsæk" is a backpack, built from "ryg" (back) and "sæk" (sack). Danes use it for school, hiking and travel. Note the plural "rygsække" and "the backpacks" as "rygsækkene". The word for a person with a backpack, "rygsækrejsende", means a backpacker.

sentence.en: I have the books in my backpack.

en rødvin.explanation: "En rødvin" is a red wine. It is made of "rød" (red) and "vin" (wine), put together as one word. In a restaurant you can say "et glas rødvin" (a glass of red wine) or "en flaske rødvin" (a bottle of red wine).

sentence.da: Jeg tager et glas **rødvin** til maden.
sentence.en: I will have a glass of red wine with the meal.

et rundstykke.explanation: "Et rundstykke" is a small round bread roll, very common for breakfast in Denmark. It is often eaten fresh from the bakery with butter, cheese or jam. Many Danes buy them at the weekend, so you say "et rundstykke" and "rundstykket".

sentence.en: I eat a bread roll with cheese.

rask.explanation: "Rask" means healthy or well again, especially after being ill. "Jeg er rask igen" means "I am well again". Danes use "at blive rask" for recovering. It also can mean quick and lively, as in "et raskt tempo" (a brisk pace). Add "t" for et-words and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "syg". "God bedring" is what you say to someone who is ill.

sentence.en: I hope you get well soon.

regn.explanation: Regn is rain. It is an et-word, so "the rain" is "regnet", and you do not say "a rain". When you want to say that it is raining, you use the verb: "Det regner" (It is raining). It is also in "en regnfrakke" (a raincoat) and "en paraply" (an umbrella) is what you bring when "det regner".

sentence.en: A lot of rain comes in the autumn.

regnvejr.explanation: "Regnvejr" is rainy weather, made from "regn" (rain) and "vejr" (weather). It is an et-word, like "vejr" itself. You often hear "Det er regnvejr" or "i regnvejr" when talking about days when you need an umbrella.

sentence.en: We stay at home in rainy weather.

rejer.explanation: "Rejer" means shrimp or prawns. One shrimp is "en reje", but you mostly hear the plural "rejer". They are popular on Danish open sandwiches ("rejemad") and in salads. "En rejemad" is a classic lunch with shrimp, egg and mayonnaise.

sentence.en: I love shrimp with lemon.

ren.explanation: "Ren" means clean, and also pure, as in "rent vand" (clean water) or "ren luft" (clean air). Add "t" for et-words ("et rent hus") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "beskidt" or "snavset" (dirty). The verb "at rengøre" means to clean, and "at gøre rent" is the everyday way to say you are cleaning the house.

sentence.en: Is your room clean?

reserveret.explanation: "Reserveret" means reserved, and it comes from the verb "at reservere" (to reserve). It stays "reserveret" with both en-words and et-words, and becomes "reserverede" when there is more than one. It is also used about people with a slightly different meaning: a "reserveret" person is reserved or a little distant.

sentence.en: This table is reserved.

resten.explanation: "Resten" means the rest, whatever is left over. It is often used with "af": "resten af maden" (the rest of the food). It has the word "the" built into the end already, so you do not add anything more. The plain form is "en rest", a remainder.

sentence.en: You can have the rest of the cake.

rig.explanation: "Rig" means rich, with a lot of money, but also rich in other things: "en rig historie" is a rich story. Add "t" for et-words ("et rigt land") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "fattig" (poor). Beware: "Riget" is a word for the kingdom, so you will see the same letters in "Danmarks rige".

sentence.en: She has become very rich.

rigtig.explanation: "Rigtig" means correct or right, as in "et rigtigt svar". It also means real or proper: "en rigtig cowboy" is a real cowboy. Used alone before another word it can mean very, in casual speech: "rigtig god" (really good). Do not mix it up with "ret", which is about rights and law. Its opposite is "forkert" (wrong).

sentence.en: Is this the right way?

ris.explanation: "Ris" means rice. It is an en-word, so "the rice" is "risen". It needs no "a" in front: "Jeg spiser ris". Be careful not to mix it up with the English "rise". You usually eat it with meat or fish, as in "kylling og ris".

sentence.en: We eat rice for dinner.

rolig.explanation: "Rolig" means calm or relaxed, and also peaceful or quiet for places. "Vær rolig" means "Stay calm" or "Calm down". Add "t" for et-words ("et roligt sted"), and "-e" for more than one. The word "roligt" is also used for "calmly": "Tal roligt". The opposite is "urolig" (restless, worried).

sentence.en: She is always so calm.

rugbrød.explanation: "Rugbrød" is rye bread, the dark, heavy bread that is typical in Denmark. It is built from "rug" (rye) and "brød" (bread). It is an et-word. It is the base for "smørrebrød", the Danish open sandwiches, and Danes eat it for lunch and breakfast.

sentence.en: I eat rye bread for lunch.

forms.en: the bakery is around the corner

forms.da: Julen er lige rundt om hjørnet
forms.en: Christmas is just around the corner

rundt om hjørnet.explanation: "Rundt om hjørnet" works literally and figuratively, just like "around the corner" in English. The words are "rundt" (around), "om" (round/about) and "hjørnet" (the corner, from "et hjørne"). Add "lige" to say "just around the corner", for something very close in place or time.

sentence.en: The post office is just around the corner.

rusland.explanation: "Rusland" is Russia. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Rusland" means "in Russia" and "til Rusland" means "to Russia". A person is "en russer" and the language is "russisk". Danish adds "-land" to many country names, as in "Finland", "Tyskland" and "Island".

sentence.en: Russia is a big country.

russisk.explanation: "Russisk" means Russian, for the language and for things from Russia. It is written with a small letter and gets no extra -t before an et-word. The person is "en russer" and the country is "Rusland".

sentence.en: He can read Russian.

rød.explanation: "Rød" means red. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et rødt hus"), and with more than one thing it gets an "e" ("røde biler"). You will see it in food too: "rødvin" is red wine and "rød pølse" is the famous Danish red hot dog.

sentence.da: Jeg kan godt lide den **røde** jakke.
sentence.en: I like the red jacket.
